title: Looking Beyond Visibility: Resolving the Temporal Structure of Continuous-Wave Four-Photon Hong-Ou-Mandel Interference
authors: Sabine Häussler, Meritxell Cabrejo-Ponce, Ana Maria Torres, Baghdasar Baghdasaryan, Karen Lozano-Mendéz, Fabian Steinlechner
abstract: Hong-Ou-Mandel interference underpins many photonic quantum information protocols and is commonly characterized by a single visibility parameter. This quantity is typically obtained by averaging over a fixed coincidence window, thereby discarding details of the underlying temporal structure that are critical in continuous-wave processes. Four-photon interference with continuous-wave sources furthermore requires photon pairs with long coherence times, which we generate in microring resonators and measure with ultrafast time-resolved detection. Here, we model and resolve their interference and temporal structure by recording all four photon arrival times and mapping their relative delays onto a three-dimensional coincidence histogram relative to a trigger detection. The resulting structure preserves relative arrival-time correlations that are usually discarded and enables post-processed optimization of coincidence windows to trade off visibility against count rate. This method provides a general benchmark for continuous-wave sources in interference-based quantum network protocols.
summary: This paper presents a novel method to characterize four-photon Hong-Ou-Mandel interference in continuous-wave sources by analyzing the full temporal structure in a three-dimensional coincidence histogram. Instead of relying on a single visibility average, the authors map relative arrival times to separate true quantum interference signals from background noise. This technique offers a general benchmark for optimizing quantum network protocols by explicitly managing the trade-off between measurement visibility and achievable count rate.
main_problem: The paper addresses the limitation of characterizing Hong-Ou-Mandel (HOM) interference using only a single visibility parameter derived from averaging over fixed coincidence windows, especially for continuous-wave (CW) sources.
main_result: By recording and analyzing all four photon arrival times in a 3D coincidence histogram, the authors resolve the underlying temporal structure, allowing for post-processed optimization of coincidence windows to trade off visibility against count rate.
method: The core method involves mapping four-fold coincidence events onto a 3D delay space using ultrafast time-resolved detection and post-processing techniques.
model_or_system: The experiment uses four-photon HOM interference generated via spontaneous four-wave mixing in microring resonators, involving two independent sources (S1 and S2) producing correlated photon pairs.
key_observables: HOM Visibility ($V_{HOM}$), the full 3D coincidence histogram, and the count rate as a function of relative arrival-time delays ($\Delta	au_{AB}, \Delta	au_{AC}, \Delta	au_{AD}$).
important_parameters: Coherence time ($	au_{coh}$), coincidence window sizes ($\Delta	au$), and the trade-off between visibility and count rate.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes detection timing jitter is shorter than the coherence time, and the model separates true four-fold events from accidental background contributions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the concept of 3D temporal mapping of four-fold interference, showing the two diagonal branches corresponding to true events (TT and RR) separated from the crossing planes representing accidental background events.
paper_structure: The paper moves from identifying the inadequacy of single-parameter characterization to developing a full 3D temporal model, detailing the separation of true quantum interference signals from classical accidental coincidences, and finally demonstrating the optimization of measurement windows.
why_interesting: This work provides a crucial, advanced diagnostic tool for quantum network protocols, moving beyond simple visibility measurements to characterize the full temporal coherence structure of multi-photon sources.

Concept of asynchronous four-fold HOM interference with two long-coherence photon-pair sources: idler photons from sources S1 (magenta) and S2 (green) interfere at a beam splitter (BS), where they can be transmitted (T) or reflected (R). The temporal delays 𝜏AB, 𝜏AC and 𝜏AD of the optical channels can be analyzed after detection, in post-processing (PP), instead of physically delaying the photons before the BS.

Distribution of possible photon detections in a four-fold HOM experiment: photon pairs generated by two independent sources (magenta and green) arrive at the detection channels with temporal correlations. We distinguish between cases in which the four-fold events originate exclusively from one photon pair from each source (a), and cases in which they arise from uncorrelated photons (b). In (a), we label these events as reflected-transmitted (RT), transmitted-reflected (TR), reflected-reflected (RR) and transmitted-transmitted (TT) photon events. Fig. 3. Temporal 3D mapping of the modeled four-fold coincidence distribution. (a) Visualization of the relative temporal delays 𝜏AB = 𝑡B −𝑡A, 𝜏AC = 𝑡C −𝑡A, 𝜏AD = 𝑡D −𝑡A as defined across the four time tagging channels. (b) Simulated 3D histogram. Here, the four-fold events are distributed along two diagonal branches, corresponding to the correlation behaviour of the RR and TT events.

Fig. 4. Two different methods to scan HOM interference. Method 1 and Method 2 are depicted in the upper (a, b) and lower (c, d) rows, respectively. The first column (a, c) shows the distributions of detection times together with the trigger detection. The second column (b, d) illustrates the scan of the coincidence window and its corresponding dimensions for each method. In Method 1, the coincidence window (red box) is scanned along a delay 𝜏(black arrow). In Method 2 (lower row), the coincidence window is shifted in two channels, resulting in a small coincidence window being translated diagonally across the three-dimensional histogram.

Fig. 5. Scheme of the accidental-scanning method, shown here as an example for XR events. One channel (here B) has an offset, while the delay of two other channels (here C and D) are scanned. Consequently, the coincidence window integrates XR-accidentals only. Similar procedures follow for the other accidental contributions.
